claims.claim: Finance is the management of money, including activities such as investing, borrowing, lending, budgeting, saving, and forecasting.
Financial management is the art and science of managing a firm's money so that it can meet its goals, and all business decisions have financial consequences.
Revenues from sales of the firm's products should be the chief source of business funding.
Businesses also raise money through debt (borrowed funds) and equity (funds raised through the sale of ownership), and financial managers seek the best balance between the two.
Money goes out to operating costs such as inventory and supplies, equipment and facilities, and wages and salaries, and to purchases that serve future operations.
Cash flow is the inflows and outflows of cash; money from sales does not always come in when it is needed to pay the bills, so financial managers track cash to ensure it is available when needed.
Cash flow is the increase or decrease in the amount of money a business has — the cash generated or consumed in a given time period.
Budgeting is the tactical implementation of a business plan: a detailed roadmap with measures, indicators, and time-based targets, and the business makes changes along the way to reach its goals.
The financial manager's key activities are financial planning (a plan projecting revenues, expenditures, and financing needs), investment (spending money), and financing (raising money).
Working capital is managed through the operating cycle: businesses sell inventory quickly, collect revenue from customers quickly, and pay bills on schedule to optimize cash flow.

A basic principle in finance is that the higher the risk, the greater the return that is required (the risk-return trade-off), and financial managers balance short- and long-term consequences of the firm's actions.
Managing finances, including proper bookkeeping and buying or leasing assets and equipment, is a standing part of running a business.

positions: Accounting view: profit is the accounting result of a period (revenue minus expenses per accounting rules) — mechanics owned by the accounting-basics sibling topic.

Finance view: cash flow is the actual money moving in and out, and it runs on its own schedule (OpenStax: money from sales does not always arrive when bills are due; CFI: cash generated or consumed in a given period).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both plainly at literacy level: profit is the accounting result, cash flow is the actual money moving, and the two move on different schedules. Accounting mechanics are left to the accounting-basics sibling; deeper cash-flow treatment belongs to the finance subject.

positions: Strict definition: net working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities.
Operating view: the money tied up in the daily cycle of inventory, customer payments, and bills (CFI's working capital cycle).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the plain operating-cycle framing at literacy level and avoids formulas and balance-sheet mechanics, which belong to the finance subject's working-capital topic.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21.
